readerTitle: The new logo cost $40,000. The rebrand cost $340,000.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (산업용 체결부품 제조사, 프로젝트 관리 앱) + 실제 기업 (Gap 2010년 로고 변경) · 가상 사례 수치는 설명용
insight: 리브랜딩의 진짜 비용은 디자인 비용이 아니라, 고객이 당신을 알아보는 데 쓰던 기억을 버리고 다시 쌓는 비용이다.
misconception: 새 로고와 이름은 디자인 비용만 들고, 더 보기 좋아지면 손해 볼 것이 없다.

sources.text: Gap, 2010년 10월 새 로고 공개 후 약 1주 만에 기존 로고로 복귀 (당시 언론 보도 및 Gap 공식 발표)
체결부품 제조사와 앱 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Gap 로고: 2010년 10월 4일경 공개, 10월 11~12일경 기존 로고 복귀 발표. 게시 전 날짜를 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "about a week"로만 적었고 매출 영향 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The new logo cost $40,000. The rebrand cost $340,000.
body: A family-owned maker of industrial bolts and fasteners has used the same dark-green boxes and blocky name for 30 years. The owner's daughter wants a fresh, modern look.
A design agency quotes $40,000. That's the price tag everyone remembers. It's also the smallest part of the bill.

image.label: Old green boxes beside new modern boxes on a warehouse shelf
image.brief: 창고 선반에 짙은 초록색 부품 상자가 가득하고, 한 칸만 새 디자인(밝은 색, 세련된 로고)의 상자. 창고 직원이 두 상자 사이에서 멈칫하는 모습. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What will the rebrand really cost?
body: The company sells $20 million a year, mostly repeat orders from distributors. It runs 25 delivery trucks, prints its own boxes and catalogs, and keeps 30% of each sale after the costs that come with it.
The agency fee is $40,000. What's the full cost of the first year?

options.feedback: This counts the design and misses everything the design has to be painted, printed and stitched onto, plus customers who lose track of you.

options.text: About $220,000, once trucks, boxes and signs are redone
options.feedback: Good catch on the rollout. But it still assumes every customer finds you just as easily under the new look.

options.text: Over $300,000, counting rollout and lost orders
options.feedback: Yes. The rollout dwarfs the fee, and a small dip in repeat orders costs more than the agency. Next card shows the math.

cards.title: Where the money goes.
body: If confused buyers let just 2% of repeat orders slip for a year, that's $400,000 in sales. At a 30% margin, the business keeps **$120,000** less. The agency fee ends up about 12% of the true cost.

breakdown.label: Packaging
breakdown.detail: New print plates, scrapped old boxes

cards.title: A rebrand makes you pay twice.
body: The **risk of rebranding** is that you pay to build a new look *and* you throw away the recognition the old one earned.

Customers don't study brands. They use quick cues, like a box color or a name, to find you in a crowded shelf, inbox or warehouse. Change the cues and some loyal buyers can't spot you, think you're a different supplier, or wonder whether the product changed too.

image.label: A customer's memory trail leading to the old box, not the new one
image.brief: 고객 머릿속 말풍선에 '초록색 상자'가 떠 있고, 점선 화살표가 선반의 옛 상자를 가리킴. 새 상자 위에는 물음표. 단순한 인포그래픽 스타일. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Gap went back in about a week.
body: In October 2010, the clothing retailer Gap replaced its familiar blue-box logo with a new design. Customers pushed back loudly online.
About a week later, Gap announced it was returning to the old logo. The new design was gone, but the money and attention spent on it were not.
The lesson isn't that the new logo was ugly. It's that people felt they owned the old one.

cards.title: Some rebrands are worth the bill.
body: A rebrand can pay off when the old brand actively hurts you: after a merger, a legal fight over the name, a scandal, or when the business has changed so much the old name misleads buyers.
Even then, you can cut the risk. Keep your strongest cue, such as the color everyone knows, and change the rest. Roll out in stages. Tell your best customers before they see it.

cards.title: The risk grows with what you've built.
body: A young business with 200 customers has little recognition to lose. For it, a better name can be cheap and smart.

The opposite mistake is real too. A brand that never updates can look tired or out of date. The question is never "change or not" in general. It's whether the gain is bigger than the recognition you give up, measured in what customers do, not what they say online.

cards.title: Now it's a project-management app.
body: Your app has a bright orange square icon that thousands of teams click every day. You've added invoicing and chat, and the old name, which mentions only tasks, feels too small.

options.text: New name, new purple icon, switch everything overnight
options.feedback: Clean and bold, but users find you by the orange square in their dock. Some will think the app vanished or was replaced.

options.text: New name, keep the orange square, tell users in the app weeks ahead
options.feedback: You fix the misleading name while keeping the cue people rely on. Warning users first turns a surprise into news.

options.text: Keep the old name and just add a tagline
options.feedback: No recognition lost, but new buyers may still read you as a task tool. You save the switching cost and keep the confusion.

cards.title: Before you rebrand, price what you're throwing away.
body: The design fee is the cheap part. The rollout and the customers who lose track of you are the real cost.
**Try it today:** list every place your logo, colors or name appear, from trucks to invoices. Then ask three regular customers how they recognize you.
